title: If viewers leave in three seconds, your video has not started yet
markdown:
# If viewers leave in three seconds, your video has not started yet

You press publish, watch the first views arrive, and open the retention graph too soon. There it is: a steep drop before you have finished the sentence you wrote to set up the video. The editing may be good. The advice may be useful. Most viewers will never find out.

![Three Hook Lab hooks for one video](https://uploads.postiz.com/WHUEBItFNl.png)

That first moment is not an introduction. It is the part of the video that has to earn the next moment.

For a short-form creator, the practical job is simple: give a stranger a reason to stop their thumb before asking them to follow a story. A hook is not a loud promise, a fake confession, or a sentence that could introduce any video. It is a specific tension that makes this video feel worth another second.

## Start with the moment that hurts

Weak openings often begin where the creator began making the video: "Today I want to talk about..." The viewer has no reason to care about that timeline. Start where their own frustration lives instead.

If the video teaches a freelance designer how to price a project, do not open with "Three pricing tips for designers." Try the pressure point: "The quote that gets accepted fastest is often the one that makes you work for free."

The second line can explain what you mean. The first line needs a live problem, a surprise, or a result the viewer can recognize. It should sound like it belongs to the footage that follows. If you could paste it onto ten unrelated clips, it is probably too broad.

## Give the hook one job

Creators often try to fit the whole video into the opening: the topic, the credentials, the lesson, the call to action, and a joke. That is a lot to ask of a few seconds. Pick one job for the hook.

It can name a mistake: "Your before-and-after videos may be losing people at the before."

It can create a useful question: "Why do some recipe videos make you hungry before the ingredient list appears?"

Or it can make a concrete promise: "I rewrote this opening so the payoff arrives before the explanation."

None of those lines guarantees attention. They do give the next shot a clear role. The viewer knows what they are waiting to learn or see.

## Write several openings before you choose one

The first hook that sounds polished is often just familiar. Familiar can be fine, but it is worth putting a few competing ideas beside it.

Take the same video and write three approaches: one that states the cost of the problem, one that challenges a common habit, and one that begins with the outcome. Read them aloud over the actual first shot. A line that works in a notes app can drag when it meets a talking head, a screen recording, or a close-up.

Then make the opening earn the edit. If the first line says a common practice is expensive, show the waste quickly. If it asks a question, answer enough of it to keep the promise moving. A hook that delays its point for too long becomes the very thing it warned against.

## Make the first frame carry some weight

Words are only part of the opening. A face reacting, a failed result, a number on screen, or the finished version of the work can make the spoken line easier to grasp. The first frame should not require viewers to decode the setting before they understand why they should stay.

This does not mean every video needs a shocked expression and giant captions. Those choices wear out quickly. It means the visual and the sentence should point at the same question. When they compete, the viewer has to do extra work at the exact moment leaving is easiest.

## Use a hook process, not a lucky sentence

The useful habit is not hunting for one magic phrase. It is building a repeatable way to find the angle that fits the clip you already have: identify the viewer's immediate problem, write distinct openings, match each one to the first frame, and keep the promise moving once the video starts.

Hook Lab is made for that early-stage problem. Use it when you have a solid video idea but the opening keeps getting treated like a preamble. Give the viewer the reason to stay before you ask for their attention.
